driver: the MIGRATION OF AI VALUE CAPTURE across the software/platform stack — if the frontier-to-open-source model catch-up window stays at ~3-6 months or compresses, raw frontier-model IP commoditizes and durable AI economics migrate to the layers ABOVE the model (application software with workflow/user/data/regulatory moats monetizing AI on proprietary data and installed workflows) and BELOW it (hyperscaler compute, cloud distribution, data gravity). The structure is PARALLEL stack layers, not a supply chain: (1) app-workflow-moat — vertical / system-of-record software with disclosed AI monetization on proprietary data or regulated workflows; (2) hyperscaler-platform — cloud/compute/distribution capturing disclosed inference and AI-deployment economics; (3) model-ip — frontier-model licensing/API economics (the LOSING side if the window holds); (4) open-ecosystem — names whose disclosed economics benefit from open-weights adoption (tooling, serving, customization); (5) silicon-ecosystem-moat — silicon vendors whose MODEL-AGNOSTIC software/developer-ecosystem bundle (programming model, software stack, developer base) captures AI economics whichever model wins — the moat, never the unit volumes. BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE IN SCOPE and the tag says which side a name sits on. Exposure must be to the MIGRATION (which layer captures AI economics), grounded in disclosed activity — NOT generic 'AI' adjacency, NOT the physical AI-datacenter build-out chain (chips/HBM/packaging/cooling/power — build-out economics of ANY shape, unit demand and pricing/mix/contract revenue alike — the ai-datacenter driver; the ONE carve-out routed here is category (5) above), NOT consumer-device AI feature mentions.

BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE IN SCOPE and the tag says which side a name sits on. Exposure must be to the MIGRATION (which layer captures AI economics), grounded in disclosed activity — NOT generic 'AI' adjacency, NOT the physical AI-datacenter build-out chain (chips/HBM/packaging/cooling/power — build-out economics of ANY shape, unit demand and pricing/mix/contract revenue alike — the ai-datacenter driver; the ONE carve-out routed here is category (5) above), NOT consumer-device AI feature mentions.

BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE IN SCOPE and the tag says which side a name sits on. Exposure must be to the MIGRATION (which layer captures AI economics), grounded in disclosed activity — NOT generic 'AI' adjacency, NOT the physical AI-datacenter build-out chain (chips/HBM/packaging/cooling/power — build-out economics of ANY shape, unit demand and pricing/mix/contract revenue alike — the ai-datacenter driver; the ONE carve-out routed here is category (5) above), NOT consumer-device AI feature mentions.

disclosed_facts.fact: HubSpot describes itself as providing an "agentic customer platform" for marketing, sales and customer service teams, built as three layers: AI-powered agents and engagement Hubs, a "Smart CRM" (the foundational context layer combining customer data with AI), and a connected partner/integration ecosystem — i.e., a system-of-record application layer with AI applied on top of customer data.

Total 2025 revenue of $3.1 billion and net income of $45.9 million from primarily subscription sales of the customer platform to 288,706 Customers in more than 135 countries; revenue is blended platform subscription revenue with no AI/agent revenue broken out.

Smart CRM is disclosed as a unified per-business data platform capturing lead and customer activity across the lifecycle, using AI to automatically enrich customer records, maintain data quality and provide unified customer context powering personalized experiences across engagement channels — AI monetized on proprietary customer data held in HubSpot's system of record.

Platform functionality disclosed includes AI-powered content creation, answer engine optimization (AEO), AI-powered configure-price-quote (CPQ) with automated billing and payment processing, and "AI agents" acting as teammates that research accounts, enrich data, answer support questions and qualify leads — AI embedded in installed customer workflows.
Stated strategic focus on mid-market B2B companies (2–2,000 employees) with the aim to "be the best at applying AI to help them grow."

Disclosed ecosystem/switching-cost elements around the platform: single login, one user interface, one unified customer view, integrations with hundreds of external applications, marketplace of integrations and templates, expert partner network, community and academy — the moat layer described qualitatively, with no attach revenue quantified.

Platform is disclosed to process billions of data points each week and to rely on "leading global cloud infrastructure providers" plus HubSpot's own automation technology to dynamically allocate capacity — HubSpot is a consumer, not a provider, of hyperscaler compute; providers unnamed and spend not quantified.

Anticipated investment areas disclosed include research and development "with respect to AI and machine learning" and data center infrastructure and service capabilities, with no amounts allocated to AI.

Risk factors disclose competitive exposure to rivals' "new or better use of evolving artificial intelligence (AI) technologies," that failure to adapt to rapidly changing AI/ML technology could make the customer platform less competitive, and that new AI-utilizing products depend on adequate R&D funding.

Q2 2026 10-Q repeats the same forward-looking AI framing — investment in R&D with respect to AI and machine learning, ability to develop new/enhanced AI applications, and competition from rivals' use of AI — plus risk that failure to adapt to AI/ML makes the platform less competitive; no AI revenue metric disclosed.

Dependence on third-party data center providers is disclosed as a risk (interruptions or delays could impair delivery of the platform), indicating reliance on external cloud/compute beneath the application layer; no contract, committed spend or provider named.
Board appointment of Gerald (Jerry) Dischler as a Class I director effective August 5, 2026, with Board expanded to eleven directors; no AI-related rationale or economics disclosed in the filing.

Data/ecosystem gravity at the application layer: the AppFolio Stack marketplace uses APIs to let customers and third parties integrate specialized external solutions into the unified AppFolio environment, with API access levels tied to plan tier (read-only in Plus, read/write in Max).

Regulated/transaction workflow positions embedded in the system of record: electronic payment services (rent, deposits, application fees, owner/vendor disbursements), FolioScreen tenant screening (credit, criminal, landlord-tenant history, income/employment/identity verification) and FolioGuard risk mitigation including renters insurance written through wholly-owned licensed subsidiary AppFolio Insurance Services, Inc. and a licensed insurance broker — regulated workflows on proprietary resident/property data.

The structure is PARALLEL stack layers, not a supply chain: (1) app-workflow-moat — vertical / system-of-record software with disclosed AI monetization on proprietary data or regulated workflows; (2) hyperscaler-platform — cloud/compute/distribution capturing disclosed inference and AI-deployment economics; (3) model-ip — frontier-model licensing/API economics (the LOSING side if the window holds); (4) open-ecosystem — names whose disclosed economics benefit from open-weights adoption (tooling, serving, customization); (5) silicon-ecosystem-moat — silicon vendors whose MODEL-AGNOSTIC software/developer-ecosystem bundle (programming model, software stack, developer base) captures AI economics whichever model wins — the moat, never the unit volumes. BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE IN SCOPE and the tag says which side a name sits on. Exposure must be to the MIGRATION (which layer captures AI economics), grounded in disclosed activity — NOT generic 'AI' adjacency, NOT the physical AI-datacenter build-out chain (chips/HBM/packaging/cooling/power — build-out economics of ANY shape, unit demand and pricing/mix/contract revenue alike — the ai-datacenter driver; the ONE carve-out routed here is category (5) above), NOT consumer-device AI feature mentions.

Model-agnostic / above-the-model positioning disclosed: the platform is deployed via Braze SDKs integrated into end-user applications, ChatGPT applications, and 'foundational LLM models through the Model Context Protocol (MCP),' plus automated connections into customer data warehouses/data platforms via the Braze Data Platform — i.e., Braze consumes external foundation models rather than monetizing model IP itself.

Monetization structure disclosed as land-and-expand subscription pricing based in large part on the number of consumers customers reach and volume of messages sent, expanding as customers add channels or purchase additional subscription products — the disclosed pricing mechanism is usage of the engagement workflow, not AI/model consumption broken out separately.

Forward-looking-statement list includes 'our use and the expected performance of artificial intelligence, or AI, and machine learning in our platform and our business and technologies' — a strategy-level AI statement with no attach revenue or layer economics attached.

The Company states the ongoing 'platform shift to AI' has elevated consumer expectations for personalization and creates new opportunities for brands, framing AI as a demand driver for its first-party-data engagement software — a market-trend assertion without disclosed AI-attributable economics.

driver: the MIGRATION OF AI VALUE CAPTURE across the software/platform stack — if the frontier-to-open-source model catch-up window stays at ~3-6 months or compresses, raw frontier-model IP commoditizes and durable AI economics migrate to the layers ABOVE the model (application software with workflow/user/data/regulatory moats monetizing AI on proprietary data and installed workflows) and BELOW it (hyperscaler compute, cloud distribution, data gravity). The structure is PARALLEL stack layers, not a supply chain: (1) app-workflow-moat — vertical / system-of-record software with disclosed AI monetization on proprietary data or regulated workflows; (2) hyperscaler-platform — cloud/compute/distribution capturing disclosed inference and AI-deployment economics; (3) model-ip — frontier-model licensing/API economics (the LOSING side if the window holds); (4) open-ecosystem — names whose disclosed economics benefit from open-weights adoption (tooling, serving, customization); (5) silicon-ecosystem-moat — silicon vendors whose MODEL-AGNOSTIC software/developer-ecosystem bundle (programming model, software stack, developer base) captures AI economics whichever model wins — the moat, never the unit volumes. BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE IN SCOPE and the tag says which side a name sits on. Exposure must be to the MIGRATION (which layer captures AI economics), grounded in disclosed activity — NOT generic 'AI' adjacency, NOT the physical AI-datacenter build-out chain (chips/HBM/packaging/cooling/power — build-out economics of ANY shape, unit demand and pricing/mix/contract revenue alike — the ai-datacenter driver; the ONE carve-out routed here is category (5) above), NOT consumer-device AI feature mentions.

driver: the MIGRATION OF AI VALUE CAPTURE across the software/platform stack — if the frontier-to-open-source model catch-up window stays at ~3-6 months or compresses, raw frontier-model IP commoditizes and durable AI economics migrate to the layers ABOVE the model (application software with workflow/user/data/regulatory moats monetizing AI on proprietary data and installed workflows) and BELOW it (hyperscaler compute, cloud distribution, data gravity). The structure is PARALLEL stack layers, not a supply chain: (1) app-workflow-moat — vertical / system-of-record software with disclosed AI monetization on proprietary data or regulated workflows; (2) hyperscaler-platform — cloud/compute/distribution capturing disclosed inference and AI-deployment economics; (3) model-ip — frontier-model licensing/API economics (the LOSING side if the window holds); (4) open-ecosystem — names whose disclosed economics benefit from open-weights adoption (tooling, serving, customization); (5) silicon-ecosystem-moat — silicon vendors whose MODEL-AGNOSTIC software/developer-ecosystem bundle (programming model, software stack, developer base) captures AI economics whichever model wins — the moat, never the unit volumes. BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE IN SCOPE and the tag says which side a name sits on. Exposure must be to the MIGRATION (which layer captures AI economics), grounded in disclosed activity — NOT generic 'AI' adjacency, NOT the physical AI-datacenter build-out chain (chips/HBM/packaging/cooling/power — build-out economics of ANY shape, unit demand and pricing/mix/contract revenue alike — the ai-datacenter driver; the ONE carve-out routed here is category (5) above), NOT consumer-device AI feature mentions.

BOTH DIRECTIONS ARE IN SCOPE and the tag says which side a name sits on. Exposure must be to the MIGRATION (which layer captures AI economics), grounded in disclosed activity — NOT generic 'AI' adjacency, NOT the physical AI-datacenter build-out chain (chips/HBM/packaging/cooling/power — build-out economics of ANY shape, unit demand and pricing/mix/contract revenue alike — the ai-datacenter driver; the ONE carve-out routed here is category (5) above), NOT consumer-device AI feature mentions.
